item.title: Ollama Structured Output vs a JSON Tool: measured tool-call loss and invented values on a local model (2026)
item.description: 18 requests on Ollama 0.20.3: 3 of 3 tool calls without a constraint, 0 of 12 with one — HTTP 200, done_reason stop, schema-valid invented values in content.
item.content:encoded:
There are two documented ways to get machine-readable output from a local Ollama model, and they look interchangeable. You can constrain the reply with format — or response_format on the OpenAI-compatible endpoint — so the decoder emits JSON that matches a schema. Or you can register a tool and let the model call it, with the tool’s result being the JSON you wanted.

The practical failure comes from doing both at once, which is a natural thing to do: keep the tools registered, and add format when a structured summary is due. On a self-hosted server the constraint wins and the tool call disappears. Nothing reports an error. The response is HTTP 200, done_reason is stop, tool_calls is absent, and content holds a schema-valid object in which the model has invented the values the tool was supposed to fetch.

This article measures that on one host and turns it into a decision plus a startup check you can run. It is not a discovery: the behaviour is filed upstream as issue #18944 and issue #13750, both open at the time of writing, and both are cited below. What those threads do not contain is a per-configuration count, so that is what this page adds.

The short answer

If your harness needs a tool result, do not put a JSON constraint on the same request. Send one request with tools and no format, let the model call, execute the tool, append the result, and only then ask for JSON in a second request that carries format and no tools.

If your harness needs a JSON object and no tool is involved, format alone is fine and does what the documentation says. The 3 control requests in this probe confirmed that path produces schema-valid content on the same model.

The dangerous configuration is the combination. Measured here, 12 requests that carried both a tool array and a JSON constraint returned 0 tool calls, 18 out of 18 requests in the whole matrix returned HTTP 200, and no response signalled the difference between “the model decided not to call” and “the server never let it call”.

What the documentation says, and what it does not say

The /api/chat reference lists format and tools as separate optional fields with no stated interaction. format is described as: “Format to return a response in. Can be json or a JSON schema”. tools is described as: “Optional list of function tools the model may call during the chat”. Both descriptions live in the request schema on the /api/chat page, and neither mentions the other.

The same separation appears on the OpenAI-compatibility side. That page ticks Tools, JSON mode and response_format as supported, in two separate checklists — Supported features carries JSON mode and Tools, Supported request fields carries response_format — with no precedence rule anywhere on the OpenAI-compatibility page.

The structured-outputs guidance is about the constraint alone: structured outputs “let you enforce a JSON schema on model responses so you can reliably extract structured data, describe images, or keep every reply consistent”, per the structured-outputs capability page. It also carries a note that “Ollama’s cloud currently does not support structured outputs”, which matters later when comparing against the cloud-vs-self-hosted report in #13750.

An absent precedence rule is an absent rule, not evidence that the fields are independent. That distinction is the whole reason this page reports counts instead of quoting the docs.

Method: 18 requests, six configurations, one small model

Everything below was measured on one host. The server reported {"version":"0.20.3"} from /api/version, and the model was qwen2.5:0.5b, already installed. The machine had 2 CPU cores and about 11.9 GB of RAM, with no GPU in use. Sampling was temperature: 0, seed: 7, stream: false, and a single user message.

The prompt was chosen so that a fabricated answer is detectable by construction: “What is the current temperature in Lisbon right now? You must use the get_weather tool to find out.” The live temperature exists only behind the tool, so any numeric temperature in content next to zero tool_calls is invented, not retrieved. The probe never executed the tool, which is deliberate: the question is not what the tool returns, it is whether the model reaches the tool path at all.

The registered tool had one required argument:

{"type": "function",
 "function": {"name": "get_weather",
              "description": "Get the current air temperature for a city from the weather service.",
              "parameters": {"type": "object",
                             "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
                             "required": ["city"]}}}

Six configurations, three repetitions each, 18 requests total:

id endpoint extra fields
a /api/chat tools only
b /api/chat tools + format = 2-field schema {city, temperature_c}
c /api/chat tools + format = enum-only schema {decision: use_tool|answer_directly}
d /api/chat tools + format = "json"
e /api/chat format = 2-field schema, no tools (control)
f /v1/chat/completions tools + response_format json_schema (same schema as b)

The exact request body for cell b, which is the one most readers will recognise from their own code:

{"model": "qwen2.5:0.5b",
 "messages": [{"role": "user",
               "content": "What is the current temperature in Lisbon right now? You must use the get_weather tool to find out."}],
 "stream": false,
 "options": {"temperature": 0, "seed": 7},
 "tools": [ ... get_weather ... ],
 "format": {"type": "object",
            "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}, "temperature_c": {"type": "number"}},
            "required": ["city", "temperature_c"]}}

Per request the run recorded the endpoint, configuration, model, repetition, HTTP status, done_reason or finish_reason, n_calls, the called function and its arguments, content length and text, whether content parsed as JSON, whether it validated against the required keys, eval_count, wall seconds, and a fabrication flag (zero calls plus a temperature-shaped value). The rows are appended to an append-only NDJSON log, results.jsonl, which is published with this article alongside the harness; every count in the tables below is a field of that file.

Result: 3 of 3 calls without a constraint, 0 of 12 with one

id configuration n HTTP 200 tool calls done_reason content parses as JSON satisfies the schema it was sent fabricated value mean wall s (load-contaminated)
a tools only 3 3 3 stop n/a (no content) n/a 0 7.61
b tools + 2-field schema 3 3 0 stop 3 3 (two-field) 3 2.66
c tools + enum schema 3 3 0 stop 3 3 (enum) 0 1.83
d tools + format: json 3 3 0 stop 3 n/a (no schema sent) 0 3.23
e schema, no tools 3 3 0 stop 3 3 (two-field) 3 7.38
f /v1 tools + response_format 3 3 0 stop 3 3 (two-field) 3 4.87

The two validity columns are separate on purpose. A per-row validator in the harness scores every reply against the two-field {city, temperature_c} reference schema, so the log records false with reason missing:city,temperature_c for cells c and d — that number says the reply did not match a reference schema those requests were never given, not that the reply was malformed. Scored against what each request actually carried, cell c’s {"decision": "use_tool"} satisfies the enum schema, and cell d was sent the bare string "json", which carries no schema to satisfy at all. The mean wall s column is labelled with its defect rather than removed: those means mix a 15.67 s cold start with warm calls of 2-5 s, so they are wall times, not a comparison of the two paths (see the latency note below).

Read the tool-call column against the configuration column. Without a constraint, every request produced a get_weather call with {"city": "Lisbon"} and an empty content. With any JSON constraint — a two-field schema, an enum-only schema, the bare string "json", or the OpenAI-compatible response_format — no request produced a call. Nine of those twelve were on /api/chat and three on /v1/chat/completions; the count is 0 in both groups.

Cell e is the important control. With no tool in the request at all, the same model under the same schema returned the same fabricated object as cell b. That is expected — there was nothing to call — and it establishes that the constrained path is the “answer directly” path by construction. Adding tools to that configuration did not reopen the tool path: b and e behaved identically apart from token counts.

eval_count separates the two cases at the wire level: 22 completion tokens for a tool-call turn without a constraint, 17 for the constrained two-field reply, 10 for the enum reply, 19 for the format: json reply. The model was generating either way; only the destination changed.

What the model produced instead

Three different shapes appeared in content, and each one defeats a different kind of check.

A schema-valid invention. Cell b returned {"city": "Lisbon", "temperature_c": 10} in all three repetitions, byte-identical. It parses, it validates, and the temperature is made up. Any harness that asserts “the final object matches the schema” passes. This is the shape that ends up in a spreadsheet.

A pseudo-call in prose. Cell d returned {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Lisbon"}} three times. The model’s intent survived intact; the server routed it into content as data instead of into tool_calls. A harness that greps content for a function name might even “work” here by accident, and a harness that expects tool_calls silently gets nothing.

A decision object that says the right thing and does nothing. The enum schema in cell c returned {"decision": "use_tool"} in all three runs. The model wanted to call the tool, said so, and the constraint left it no way to express that as a call. The schema was satisfied; the request was not.

Cell f adds a detail worth noting for anyone comparing endpoints. On /v1/chat/completions the fabricated temperatures were 14.5, 17 and 18.2 — three different invented values under temperature: 0 and seed: 7, where the native endpoint returned the same byte string three times. Reproducibility settings are not carried identically across the two surfaces, so a determinism argument built on one endpoint does not transfer to the other.

Prior art: the behaviour is filed upstream

Issue #18944, opened 2026-10-11 and open at the time of writing, reports it for qwen3.5:9b on /api/chat: “When using the /api/chat endpoint and the format is set to json, then the model is unable to use any tool calls. It might either try to use the tool call in the response or it will make something up in the response.” Both observed shapes in this probe — pseudo-call in content, invented values — are named in that report.

The thread also documents the reasoning, and the correction to it. A maintainer first replied that “a tool call does not confirm to a JSON schema, so the model can’t generate the tool call”. The reporter then noted that tools worked with a JSON format until roughly version 0.32, and the maintainer agreed that his first comment reflected older versions: it worked for thinking models up to 0.34.3, and the behaviour changed in 0.34.4 with a linked pull request, #18479. Those version numbers come from the thread; nothing on this host can confirm them, and the server measured here reports 0.20.3 while still reproducing the failure. No regression boundary is asserted anywhere in this article.

Issue #13750, opened 2026-01-16 and open at the time of writing, states the precedence directly: “When both tools and response_format are present in the request, response_format takes complete priority over tools. The model is forced to generate a hallucinated JSON response conforming to the schema without ever considering tool calls.” The reporter also reports that the same request works on Ollama.com, which conflicts with the current documentation note that the cloud does not support structured outputs. Both statements are recorded here as reported; they are not reconciled into a claim.

None of the comments in either thread reports a per-configuration call count, which is the gap this page fills. It is also why the article is framed as a measured decision and a detection rule, not as a bug discovery.

The detection rule a harness should run

finish_reason cannot distinguish a suppressed call from a legitimate one. Neither can schema validation: cell b passed it while inventing the number. The failure is visible only in the relationship between the request’s shape and the response’s shape, which means detection belongs at the configuration level, not per response.

The cheap version is a startup canary: send the same deterministic request twice, once with tools only and once with tools plus format, and compare the call counts. If the unconstrained request calls and the constrained one never does, the server has this behaviour and every “tools + format” code path in the harness is dead.

def canary(base, model, tool, schema, prompt):
    def ask(extra):
        body = {"model": model, "stream": False,
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                "options": {"temperature": 0, "seed": 7},
                "tools": [tool], **extra}
        req = urllib.request.Request(base + "/api/chat",
                                     data=json.dumps(body).encode(),
                                     headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120) as r:
            d = json.loads(r.read())
        return len((d.get("message") or {}).get("tool_calls") or []), d

    bare = ask({})[0]
    constrained, resp = ask({"format": schema})
    if bare and not constrained:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "tools+format suppresses tool calls on this server: bare=%d constrained=%d "
            "done_reason=%r content=%r" % (
                bare, constrained, resp.get("done_reason"),
                ((resp.get("message") or {}).get("content") or "")[:120]))

The canary costs two requests and fails at boot instead of six weeks later in a spreadsheet. Keep it alongside your version check: the behaviour is version- and model-scoped, so a server upgrade or a model swap is exactly when it should run again.

A per-response check is possible but weaker, because “the model correctly decided not to call” is indistinguishable from “the call was suppressed” without knowing whether the prompt required the tool. If you must do it per response, make provenance explicit: require that every fact field in the final object carry the tool_call_id that produced it, and reject a reply whose fact fields have no tool provenance. That converts cell b from a pass into a loud failure without needing to infer intent.

Decision table

Your need Configuration Status in this probe
Final JSON, no tool involved format alone Measured: schema-valid content in 3 of 3 (e).
A tool result, then more work tools only on the call turn Measured: calls in 3 of 3 (a).
Tool result and a JSON summary in one flow two requests: call with tools, then summarise with format and no tools Not measured here. Follows from the suppression above and is the obvious workaround, but treat it as a hypothesis until your own canary confirms it.
Both fields in one request none — treat the tool as unavailable Measured: 0 calls in 12 of 12 constrained requests; invented values in 6.

The two-turn path is the one readers will reach for, and it is worth being blunt that this run did not execute it: no second arm, no final-output validity rate. What this run establishes is the boundary that makes the two-turn design necessary — an unconstrained call turn works, and any constraint on that same turn does not.

Wall times: recorded, not a latency comparison

The title of this page does not claim a latency result, and this section is why. The mean wall times in the table are contaminated by model load. The first a request took 15.67 s while the process was loading qwen2.5:0.5b onto 2 CPU cores; the next two took 2.5 s and 4.7 s. With n=3 per cell, a single cold start moves the mean by seconds, and the constrained cells look faster partly because they emit fewer completion tokens (17 versus 22). Do not read those means as a comparison of the two paths. A real comparison needs a warmed model, interleaved repetitions, and many more than three samples per cell.

Limitations

One model (qwen2.5:0.5b), one server version (0.20.3), one host, one prompt wording, one turn, three repetitions per cell. A 0-in-3 result is compatible with a truly zero rate and with a substantial rate, so the claim is “no call in 12 constrained requests on this configuration”, not “this never happens anywhere”. The upstream reports show the same shape on qwen3.5:9b and on 0.14.1 and 0.16.1, which is why the behaviour looks server-side rather than model-specific, but no larger model was run here.

The tool was never executed, so no real temperature exists to compare the invented one against; fabrication is established by the question being unanswerable without the tool, not by diffing against a live reading. The exact invented number is model- and prompt-specific.

No second prompt wording was run, so the effect is shown not to depend on sampling (identical output across repetitions at temperature: 0) but not shown to be independent of phrasing. No two-turn loop was measured.

How to reproduce it

The harness behind the table is a single stdlib-only Python file: one urllib POST per request, an NDJSON append per response, and a wall-clock budget that stops the run and keeps partial rows. It is published with the run record, along with a test that exercises it without a model:

file what it is
probe.py the matrix harness: six configurations, both endpoints, PROBE_MODELS / PROBE_REPS / PROBE_DEADLINE_S from the environment
results.jsonl the 18 rows behind the table, one JSON object per request
summary.json per-configuration counts and means, derived from those rows
run_meta.json model, repetitions, deadline and the host server version reported at run time
fixture_test.py stdlib mock server that replays one tool-calling and one constrained reply, then runs the harness against it
fixture_output.txt the recorded output of that test: 14 assertions, 0 failed 
PROBE_MODELS=qwen2.5:0.5b PROBE_REPS=3 PROBE_DEADLINE_S=140 \
  python3 probe.py

Keep the two kinds of check apart, because they establish different things. The fixture test proves the harness mechanics — that the request bodies are shaped as described, that each response becomes one NDJSON row with the recorded fields, that the validator scores a reply against the two-field reference schema, and that the canary below raises when a call is suppressed. It runs against a mock server on 127.0.0.1 with a fixed replay rule and no model, so it is not evidence about any Ollama build and says nothing about tool-call rates. The table is the live part: 18 requests against Ollama 0.20.3 with qwen2.5:0.5b on 2026-11-10, and only that run is evidence about the server.

To repeat the live run, point the harness at a server on 127.0.0.1:11434, or change one constant for a remote host. A fresh run either reproduces the table or shows that the installed version no longer behaves this way — which is the result worth having either way, since the upstream thread’s own version attribution is unresolved.

If you arrived here from a build guide, the surrounding pieces are in the local agents guide, the two-path overview is in the function-calling guide, the library-level decision this page does not repeat is in the structured-output guide, and the endpoint reference is the Ollama API integration guide.

Two neighbouring silent failures are worth telling apart from this one. A tool call can also vanish through conversation-history replay, with a different signature: empty content, no tool_calls, non-zero eval_count, covered in the history-corruption write-up. And a prompt that overflows the context window truncates silently, which produces the same “nothing useful came back” experience from the input side, covered in the context-truncation note. Neither is this constraint path; the equivalent defect on a different local server, where the streaming parser corrupts calls, is in the vLLM parser write-up.

The one-line version: a JSON constraint and a registered tool are not two ways to the same end. On a self-hosted Ollama server measured here, the constraint wins silently, the call disappears, and the object that comes back is valid, plausible, and invented.

item.title: Ollama Thread Tuning on CPU: Measuring Where More Threads Stop Helping Token Generation (2026)
item.description: num_thread is a load-time Runner option whose API default is 0, and Ollama's documented configuration has no OLLAMA_NUM_THREAD variable. On a 2-vCPU host a fixed sweep measured 13.25 generation tok/s at one thread, about 22.9 at two in the fast-mode rows, and 0.56-0.65 at four, with prompt evaluation timed separately from generation.
item.content:encoded:
You follow the usual advice: the local model server is using all your cores, so you pin the thread count to the number of cores and expect token generation to speed up. On a 2-vCPU box the opposite happens. The same 66-token prompt that produced 55 tokens in about 4.5 seconds with one thread took 109 seconds with four, and two later requests at that setting, bounded at 90 seconds in the second window, never returned at all. Both completed requests returned HTTP 200 with an ordinary response body; nothing in them announced that the setting was wrong.

The advice is a number without a measurement behind it, and it never says which of the two timed phases it is supposed to change. Ollama reports prompt evaluation and token generation as separate durations, and they behave differently — but almost every “tokens per second” figure people quote divides output tokens by total wall time, which mixes the two. This article shows what num_thread actually is in Ollama 0.20.3, what the server’s own default did on a small shared host, and a one-request-at-a-time sweep that separates the phases. It also reports the negative results: one cell was too noisy to average, four threads collapsed throughput instead of improving it, and eight threads was never measured.

The knob exists; the environment variable does not

num_thread is a field on the Runner option struct in Ollama’s Go API, alongside num_ctx, num_batch and num_gpu, and it is accepted in the options object of a generate request (ollama/api/types.go). The same file shows the default Ollama’s own API layer fills in: NumThread: 0, // let the runtime decide. Zero is not a thread count; it is a request to the runtime to choose.

The variable that articles and forum posts tell you to export, OLLAMA_NUM_THREAD, is not in the server’s documented configuration. The FAQ’s environment-variable list documents OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS, OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL, OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE and the host/model settings, and contains no thread-count variable (Ollama FAQ); the envconfig package that parses those variables on the main branch has no thread setting either (envconfig/config.go). Absence from these files is not proof that the binary ignores an unknown variable, and older releases may differ, but it does mean the widely repeated export is not a documented control surface. The supported way to set the value is per request, in options.

Control Where it lives Default What it changes
num_thread options object of /api/generate, load-time Runner field 0 (“let the runtime decide”) Worker threads used by the loaded model
OLLAMA_NUM_THREAD Not present in the FAQ list or envconfig — Nothing documented
OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL Server environment variable 1 How many requests one model processes at once
OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE Server environment variable 512 Requests queued before new ones are rejected

What the default resolves to, and why this article will not name it

It is tempting to answer “four”, because llama.cpp’s context parameters default both thread counts to GGML_DEFAULT_N_THREADS (llama-context.cpp), and GGML_DEFAULT_N_THREADS is defined as 4 (ggml.h). That is llama.cpp’s own untouched default. It is not a statement about what the Ollama server passes down after it receives NumThread: 0, and the measurement below contradicts reading it that way.

llama.cpp also keeps two independent counts, and the header says so: n_threads is used “for generation (single token)” and n_threads_batch “for prompt and batch processing (multiple tokens)” (llama.h). A single requested num_thread therefore has to be mapped onto two different worker pools, which is one reason a single “tokens/s” number cannot describe the effect.

On this host the default behaved like the two-thread setting, not the four-thread one. With num_thread omitted, two requests produced 21.37 and 23.61 generation tok/s (median 22.49, CV 5.0%, rows at 2026-11-04T17:18:03Z and 17:18:04Z) while an explicit four-thread request in the same window managed 0.65 tok/s. Four threads cannot be the setting that produced the default rows — the gap is roughly 35x. What the data cannot do is separate the rule “use nproc” from “use min(4, nproc)”, because both evaluate to 2 on a 2-vCPU machine. So the honest statement is: the default runs in the two-thread band here, the four-thread constant does not describe it, and the exact resolution rule stays unresolved.

Method

The host is a shared 2-vCPU Neoverse-N1 build machine with 11,927 MB of RAM, running Ollama 0.20.3 and kernel 6.17.0-1019-oracle. The model is qwen2.5:0.5b Q4_K_M, digest a8b0c51577010a279d933d14c2a8ab4b268079d44c5c8830c0a93900f1827c67, loaded with num_ctx 2048, temperature 0, seed 42 and keep_alive 5m. Two fixed prompts were used: a 66-token short prompt and a 606-token long prompt, both counted by the server’s own prompt_eval_count. num_predict was 96 for the explicit-thread cells and 32 for the default cells and one completed four-thread request, so generation tok/s normalises across them but wall-clock durations do not.

num_thread was passed in the request options rather than set globally, so every cell used the same resident model and the shared daemon was never restarted. Requests ran strictly one at a time, each a synchronous HTTP call, with a 180-second client timeout in the round-0 window and 90 seconds in the round-1 window — which is why the round-0 four-thread request is recorded as completing in 109.4 seconds while the two round-1 four-thread requests are recorded as timed out; no background process, no shell job control, no signal to the service. Rows were appended to separate files per window, and nothing was deleted or rewritten between rounds. The only load-average reading attached to an analysed round-0 request is 4.78 at 16:32:58Z, the start of the invocation that produced the four-thread row; a 4.04 reading was written at 16:23:11Z, at the end of the rejected dedicated-instance attempt and 32 seconds before the first analysed request, so it is a pre-window reading and not an end-of-window one. The round-1 rows store 4.13-4.69 next to the individual requests, against 2 runnable vCPUs.

The raw rows, probe scripts and method notes from both windows are kept in the author’s private run record and are not published as downloadable files; the request body, host specification and field list in this article are everything needed to rerun the same sweep, and the numbers below are reported with their timestamps so they can be checked against that record.

Results

Twenty-one records across two windows on 2026-11-04 (16:23-16:34 UTC and 17:14-17:18 UTC). All figures are generation tokens per second, computed from the server’s eval_count and eval_duration, never from wall time. Every CV in the table is the population standard deviation divided by the mean of the rows listed for that cell, so the column is comparable across cells.

Cell (2 vCPU host) Requests Median generation tok/s Range CV
1 thread, 66-token prompt 3 13.25 13.12-13.30 0.6%
1 thread, 606-token prompt 3 11.20 11.18-11.21 0.1%
2 threads, 66-token prompt, fast mode 3 22.88 22.48-23.00 1.0%
2 threads, 66-token prompt, slow mode 3 3.25 1.81-3.72 not averaged
2 threads, 606-token prompt 3 18.58 18.49-18.62 0.3%
Default (no num_thread) 2 22.49 21.37-23.61 5.0%
4 threads, 66-token prompt 2 (+2 timeouts) 0.60 0.56-0.65 7.8%
8 threads 0 not measured — —

Two threads beat one on both prompt sizes in this sample: 13.25 to 22.88 tok/s on the short prompt and 11.20 to 18.58 tok/s on the long one, which is what you would expect when two real cores are given two worker threads. The size of the short-prompt gain should not be averaged — see the next section — and the long-prompt ratio (1.66x for twice the threads) is the more trustworthy of the two because that cell was stable.

The two-thread short cell split into two modes

Six short-prompt rows at two threads exist across the two windows, three per window: 22.48, 22.88 and 22.99 tok/s in one mode, and 1.81, 3.25 and 3.72 tok/s in the other. The combined CV of those six rows is 77%, far past the 15% ceiling this experiment set for itself, so no averaged 1-to-2 gain is published from that cell. Both modes are real observations from the same server and model, and the fast mode matches the default cell’s band, which is why the table reports them as two populations.

The plausible mechanism is host contention, not thread count: two of the three slow rows recorded load averages of 4.58 and 4.69 on 2 vCPUs, and the third stores no load average at all, while a neighbour taking the cores leaves the model’s two threads runnable but not scheduled. The operational consequence is that on a shared box you cannot compare a thread setting against a baseline taken minutes earlier and attribute the difference to threads. Record load average next to every row, and if your repetitions split into two clusters, report the clusters instead of a mean.

Four threads on a two-core host collapses throughput

Oversubscription did not produce a plateau. It produced a cliff. Two completed requests at num_thread: 4 measured 0.56 tok/s (55 tokens in 109.4 s wall clock; the 4.78 load average was recorded at the window start, 16:32:58Z, two minutes before this row, which stores no load average of its own) and 0.65 tok/s (32 tokens in 50.9 s, load average 4.13, 17:16:51Z), with two more requests at the same setting in the second window timing out at 90 seconds. The collapse was reproduced in two windows about 42 minutes apart, on the same model digest and the same server instance, so it is not one bad request.

The magnitude is contention-dependent: both windows had load above the two available cores, so this measures oversubscribed threads on an oversubscribed host, which is the realistic condition for a shared CPU box but not a clean single-tenant figure. The direction is what the data supports — on a 2-vCPU machine, asking for twice the cores costs roughly 35-40x generation throughput relative to the server’s own default, and some requests never complete. If you set num_thread from nproc on a machine where nproc already counts hyperthreads or is shared with other work, this is the failure you are signing up for.

Why a single tokens/s number hides the effect

Ollama’s generate response reports prompt_eval_duration as “time spent evaluating uncached prompt tokens”, eval_duration as “time spent generating tokens”, and prompt_eval_cached_count alongside them (/api/generate). Divide output tokens by total time and you mix prefill, generation and model load into one figure.

The clearest example is the first long-prompt request at one thread: 42.70 s total, of which 34.87 s was prompt evaluation and only 7.52 s was the 84 generated tokens. Generation was 11.18 tok/s; dividing 84 tokens by 42.70 s gives 1.97 tok/s, a 5.7x understatement of the thing you were trying to tune. The second identical request finished in 7.96 s because 606 prompt tokens came back from cache (prompt_eval_duration dropped from 34.87 s to 0.10 s). Any sweep that repeats one prompt without noticing prompt_eval_cached_count will “discover” a 5x speedup that is just the cache warming up.

Counting the phases separately is also the only way to see that the four-thread collapse hits both. In the long-prompt cell, prefill went from 17.4 tok/s at one thread (606 tokens in 34.87 s) to 31.1 tok/s at two (606 tokens in 19.50 s), a factor of 1.79, while generation went from 11.20 to 18.58 tok/s, a factor of 1.66 — so “prompt evaluation scales differently from generation” was not observed here; both phases responded to the same doubling, roughly equally. What the separation does buy you is attribution: at four threads the 66-token prompt evaluated at roughly 44 tok/s (1.50 s for 66 tokens) against roughly 873 tok/s at one thread, about 20x slower, while generation fell from 13.25 to 0.60 tok/s. Prefill is not immune to oversubscription just because it uses the batch worker pool.

What to set, and when threads are the wrong lever

On a 2-vCPU host, the measured default was already at the two-thread band and matched an explicit two-thread request; there was nothing to gain by setting the value and a large loss at four. Leaving num_thread unset was the correct configuration here, and the null result is the finding worth keeping.

On 4- or 8-core machines the same protocol transfers but the conclusion does not: measure nproc, run three repetitions at one, nproc and 2 x nproc threads with a fixed prompt, discard a warm-up request, and compare medians only if every cell’s CV stays under about 15%. Past nproc, expect degradation rather than a plateau — the plateau in this data is not “more threads stop helping”, it is “more threads than cores is actively harmful”. If the reason you started tuning is that a second agent session is waiting for the first, thread count is the wrong lever: the requests are serialised by the server’s parallel-slot setting, which is a separate queueing problem described in two agent sessions against one local model server. If you are squeezing a model into memory, that is a context and KV-cache budget, not a scheduling one (VRAM and KV-cache budget).

The request that produced each row above is small enough to paste into a terminal, with the thread count as the only variable:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate -d '{
  "model": "qwen2.5:0.5b",
  "prompt": "<fixed prompt>",
  "stream": false,
  "keep_alive": "5m",
  "options": {"num_thread": 2, "num_ctx": 2048, "num_predict": 96,
              "temperature": 0, "seed": 42}
}'

Record eval_count, eval_duration, prompt_eval_count, prompt_eval_duration, prompt_eval_cached_count, total_duration and the host load average for every request; compute generation tok/s as eval_count / (eval_duration / 1e9). Omit the num_thread key entirely for the default cell — passing 0 is not the same as omitting it, since 0 is what the API substitutes when the field is absent, and the comparison you care about is what the server does when nobody asks. Delete one warm-up request per cell before collecting, and never compare a cached prompt against an uncached one. Model choice on a CPU-only host is a bigger lever than any of this and is covered in best local LLM models and best Ollama coding models; the API surface itself is in the Ollama API integration guide, and the agent-side tuning block most readers arrive from is in Aider with Ollama.

Limitations

No eight-thread cell exists. Every request above two threads either hit the client timeout of the window that ran it (90 seconds, in the second window) or completed at about 0.6 tok/s, so a further cell would have consumed the remaining measurement budget without producing a distinguishable result; nothing in this article implies eight threads were measured. The two-thread short cell is bimodal and is reported as two modes, not a mean, and neither round reached the nine repetitions the original plan targeted. Host load averaged above the two available cores for much of both windows, so absolute throughput is not a single-tenant number and the four-thread collapse magnitude would be smaller on an idle machine. The effective default thread count could not be resolved from source or from a readable server log, and this host cannot distinguish the two candidate rules because both give 2. All source checks are against main-branch files and current documentation read on 2026-11-04 and re-checked on 2026-11-19, not a tagged 0.20.3 release tarball; every quoted fact was present verbatim in both readings, though the files’ bytes and line numbers changed between them, so a later main-branch change could still invalidate a quotation. Every figure above comes from a two-window local measurement; no vendor benchmark is quoted, and the observation that both phases respond to thread count rests on one prompt size and one 0.5B model, so a larger model or a different prefill length could still split them.

item.title: The Chat Template or a Built-in Parser Decides Whether Ollama Gives You a Tool Call
item.description: Ollama 0.20.3 returned a read_file call with .Tools in the chat template and HTTP 400 "does not support tools" without it — unless a built-in parser grants tools. The check, the probe and the fix.
item.content:encoded:
You pass a tools array to /api/chat, the call fails, and nothing in the response explains why. On ollama 0.20.3 the failure is a bare HTTP 400 whose message is registry.ollama.ai/library/<model>:latest does not support tools, which names the model and points at the wrong layer. On a server old enough to have no tools field in its chat request at all — v0.2.0 and earlier — that JSON key is dropped unread, so the same call returns HTTP 200 with a prose answer and no tool_calls field, and the client reports “the model ignored the schema”.

The direct answer, measured on one host and readable in the pinned source: on a build that configures no built-in tool parser, whether it can emit a tool call is decided by its chat TEMPLATE, not by the model name, family or parameter count. A template that references .Tools declares the variable tools, the server grants the build the tools capability, and the tool schemas get rendered into the prompt. Remove that block and keep the identical weights in the identical blob, and the server refuses the request before the model ever runs.

The qualifier is not decoration. The same function in v0.20.3 grants the tools capability on either of two branches — slices.Contains(v, "tools") || (builtinParser != nil && builtinParser.HasToolSupport()) — and builtinParser is resolved from m.Config.Parser. At that tag five built-in parsers (cogito, gemma4, deepseek3, lfm2, ministral) return true from HasToolSupport(), so a build whose Modelfile selects one of them has tools with no .Tools variable anywhere in its template. The build tested here selects none of them: its template-stripped derivative was refused, which shows the capability came from the template and from nothing else. Every measurement below therefore describes template-branch builds only. The probe does not speak for parser-configured builds, and no such build was run here.

Thirty-second check, before you change model

Two commands answer the yes/no question for any local build:

ollama show --modelfile qwen2.5:0.5b | sed -n '/TEMPLATE """/,/"""/p' | grep -c '\.Tools'
ollama show qwen2.5:0.5b | sed -n '/Capabilities/,+3p'

The first prints a non-zero count for a build whose template contains a .Tools block. The second prints the capability list the server has derived — the list it later checks a tools request against. Read them in that order. A count of 0 with no tools in the list means no prompt engineering will help: the request will be refused or the schema will never be rendered. A count of 0 with tools in the list means a built-in parser is supplying the capability rather than the template, so the count tells you nothing about whether tools work; only a request does. ollama show --modelfile is where you look for the parser the build selected.

Reading the flag is necessary, not sufficient. A build flagged tools can still answer in prose if the weights are weak, if the schema is malformed, or if the client sends stream: true and the parser drops the call. The flag tells you the layer is capable; only a request tells you whether a call comes out.

The three builds and their rows

One host, CPU only, 2 vCPU, 11 GB RAM, ollama version is 0.20.3, model qwen2.5:0.5b (digest a8b0c5157701, 397 MB, Q4_K_M, already resident). The two derivatives were built FROM qwen2.5:0.5b with the same SYSTEM line; probe-notools:latest deletes only the {{- if .Tools }}...{{- end }} conditional and the or .Tools clause in the message wrapper, and probe-faketools:latest re-adds the literal word “tools” as one prose sentence, with no .Tools reference.

Build .Tools in TEMPLATE Tools sent HTTP Response class prompt_eval_count
qwen2.5:0.5b yes yes, 2 runs 200 tool_calls: one read_file 180
qwen2.5:0.5b yes no, 2 runs 200 prose, no call 51
probe-notools:latest no yes, 2 runs 400 refused before generation not returned
probe-notools:latest no no, 2 runs 200 prose, no call 52
probe-faketools:latest no (prose “tools” only) yes, 2 runs 400 refused before generation not returned

Every tools-carrying request against a build without the block came back 400, twice out of twice, with does not support tools in the error. The same request against the parent build produced a read_file call both times, with message.content empty and prompt_eval_count: 180.

What the token count proves

Without a tools array, the identical messages and options produced prompt_eval_count: 51. With the one-tool schema they produced 180. The delta is the receipt that the schema text actually entered the prompt instead of being accepted by the API and quietly discarded. That is the cheap field to read when a client says “the model ignores my tools”: if prompt_eval_count is unchanged with and without the array, the schema never reached the model, and the fault is above the weights.

prompt_eval_count is a token count, not a diff of the rendered text, so it shows extra input was rendered, not that the schema was rendered well. The extracted template for the parent build is published with this post (linked under Reproduction), so you can confirm the exact strings yourself instead of inferring them from a count.

The probe you can rerun

The measured runs used a stdlib-only script that extracts the template, builds the derivative, posts the same payload to /api/chat and classifies the answer. The essential loop is small enough to paste into a file:

import json, urllib.request
payload = {"model": "qwen2.5:0.5b", "stream": False,
           "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Read /etc/hostname with the read_file tool."}],
           "options": {"temperature": 0, "seed": 7, "num_predict": 128},
           "tools": [{"type": "function", "function": {
               "name": "read_file", "description": "Read a file from disk.",
               "parameters": {"type": "object", "required": ["path"],
                              "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}}}}}]}
req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/chat",
                             data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
                             headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
try:
    body = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120).read()
    d = json.loads(body); msg = d.get("message", {})
    cls = "tool_calls" if msg.get("tool_calls") else "prose_no_call"
    print(cls, d.get("prompt_eval_count"), msg.get("content", "")[:120])
except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
    print("refused", e.code, e.read().decode()[:200])

Run it twice, then rerun it without the tools key and compare prompt_eval_count. Repeat after every re-pull, re-quant or ollama create, because the digest and the template can change together.

Which layer is at fault

Symptom Layer Check Fix
400 does not support tools template / capability gate ollama show --modelfile <model> has no .Tools block add a .Tools block to the Modelfile, ollama create a new tag
200, prose, prompt_eval_count unchanged without/with tools template same as above same as above
200, prose, prompt_eval_count higher with tools model or prompt schema reached the prompt strengthen the instruction, check the model actually learned the format
200, tool_calls present in raw JSON, absent in your client client parser curl the endpoint directly fix the streaming/JSON parser, not the model

The last row is the reason to always test with a direct HTTP call before blaming the model: a framework that parses only content will report “no tool call” for a perfectly good response.

If the call does come out and the trouble starts on the next turn — the assistant turn comes back with empty content, no tool_calls and an eval_count above zero, or an argument is returned retyped — you are past this layer; that failure is diagnosed in the history-rewriting write-up. If instead the open question is terminology — what a tool schema, a tool_calls message and a tool result are, and where each one sits in the request — start with the function-calling and tool-use guide, which maps each provider’s call and result pair and shows how to keep that pair intact.

What the pinned source says

In v0.20.3 the capability list is computed from the template and from the configured parser, not from the model name. The server warns if the template does not parse, then appends the tools capability when either the template’s declared variables contain tools or the parser named by m.Config.Parser reports tool support — server/images.go at v0.20.3:

builtinParser := parsers.ParserForName(m.Config.Parser)
// Check for tools capability
v, err := m.Template.Vars()
if err != nil {
    slog.Warn("model template contains errors", "error", err)
}
if slices.Contains(v, "tools") || (builtinParser != nil && builtinParser.HasToolSupport()) {
    capabilities = append(capabilities, model.CapabilityTools)
}

Vars() returns the identifiers the template actually references, lower-cased and de-duplicated — template/template.go on main walks the parsed root nodes and collects identifiers, which is why a sentence containing the word “tools” contributes nothing: prose is not an identifier. That is the first branch, and it matches the measured control: probe-faketools:latest, which configures no parser, was refused in both runs.

The second branch is read from source here, not measured. parsers.ParserForName(m.Config.Parser) resolves whatever parser the build selected, and at v0.20.3 HasToolSupport() returns true in model/parsers/cogito.go, gemma4.go, deepseek3.go, lfm2.go and ministral.go. A build that selects one of those gets tools in its capability list with no .Tools in its template, so a probe that only inspects the template would classify it as incapable when the server accepts its tools requests. The fetched excerpts and their file hashes are in the parser-branch excerpt published with this post.

The chat handler takes the other half of the decision. It appends the tools capability to the requested set whenever the request carries a non-empty tools array, then asks the scheduler for a runner with that set — server/routes.go at v0.20.3:

caps := []model.Capability{model.CapabilityCompletion}
if len(req.Tools) > 0 {
    caps = append(caps, model.CapabilityTools)
}

So the API always accepts the field and always asks for the capability; the refusal happens when the build’s own capability list cannot satisfy it. The message itself is assembled in the same file as the check: CheckCapabilities joins a sentinel does not support with tools into one error, which is how a template property ends up reported as a model property. The 400 status is what the probe observed on the wire in 0.20.3; treat the exact wording as an observation of this build, not as a documented API contract.

The API documentation is not where you learn this. docs/api.md at v0.20.3 shows a tools array in a /api/chat example and says nothing about which builds accept it, so a developer reading the docs reasonably concludes that the field is universally supported and that a model which “ignores” it is at fault.

Newer code on main, read on 2026-11-02 with no binary built or run here, is looser: the chat-template path grants the tools capability on a plain substring test for tools or tool_call rather than on declared variables — server/images.go on main:

func chatTemplateHasToolSupport(chatTemplate string) bool {
	return strings.Contains(chatTemplate, "tools") || strings.Contains(chatTemplate, "tool_call")
}

That is a source-level observation about newer code, not a measurement: no main-branch binary was built or run here, so nothing is claimed about whether probe-faketools:latest would be accepted by it. If you are on a newer build, run the probe rather than assuming either rule applies.

Limits

Single host, CPU only, one 0.5B model and two derivative builds. Everything above is a behaviour observation — did a call happen, was the request refused — and wall times from these runs (0.1 s to 54 s, unloaded model on 2 vCPU) are logged in the run record but not claimed as latency. No GPU, no larger model and no parser-configured build were tested, so nothing here says how often a bigger flagged build produces a well-formed call, and nothing here measures the HasToolSupport() branch at runtime. The version where the tools field and the capability gate first appeared was not bisected, but the window is narrow: api/types.go at v0.2.0 has no Tools field in ChatRequest at all, while server/routes.go at v0.2.8 already appends the tools capability when the request carries a non-empty array. On a build before that window the key is dropped by the JSON decoder and the reply is prose with HTTP 200 — read from source for this post, not measured on this host, and not offered as a claim about any particular release in between.

Reproduction

The run record, the control run, all three Modelfiles and the extracted templates for the positive and negative cases are published with this post. These are local first-party measurements on the host described above, not vendor benchmarks or third-party downloads:

  • Probe driver that produced the rows (edit the EV path at the top to your own evidence directory): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/ollama-chat-template-tool-support-probe-2026/probe_tool_template.py
  • Run record for the parent and probe-notools builds, with per-run status, response class, token counts and timestamps: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/ollama-chat-template-tool-support-probe-2026/probe-run.json
  • Control run for the prose-mention build: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/ollama-chat-template-tool-support-probe-2026/probe-faketools.json
  • Modelfile for the negative case, with only the .Tools conditional removed: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/ollama-chat-template-tool-support-probe-2026/Modelfile.notools
  • Extracted template of the negative derivative, with the .Tools block absent: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/ollama-chat-template-tool-support-probe-2026/template-probe-notools.txt
  • Full ollama show --modelfile dump for the parent build, the file the derivative was cut from: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/ollama-chat-template-tool-support-probe-2026/modelfile-qwen2.5-0.5b.txt
  • Extracted TEMPLATE of the parent build — the positive case behind the higher prompt token count: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/ollama-chat-template-tool-support-probe-2026/template-qwen2.5-0.5b.txt
  • Modelfile for the prose-mention control, where the word “tools” sits in a sentence and .Tools appears nowhere: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/ollama-chat-template-tool-support-probe-2026/Modelfile.faketools
  • Parser-branch source excerpt for v0.20.3, with the capability condition and the five HasToolSupport() returns plus per-file sha256: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/ollama-chat-template-tool-support-probe-2026/upstream-parser-tool-support-v0.20.3.txt

The practical conclusion is one habit: before you debug a client, a prompt or a model choice, ask the build whether it can accept tools at all — read the capability list, then send one tools request and read prompt_eval_count. If neither the template nor a configured parser can grant the capability, swap the template or the parser, not the model: the weights were never the problem.
